script.t: Tonight we're asking whether neuroscience has disproved free will. Alan, you've argued that it has, or at least that it's seriously undermined the idea.

I'd say it's undermined a certain naive picture of free will, yes. The classic starting point is a set of experiments conducted by Benjamin Libet in the 1980s. Participants were asked to flex their wrist whenever they felt like it and to note, using a special clock, the moment they became aware of deciding to move. Meanwhile, electrodes recorded their brain activity. What Libet found was that a build-up of electrical activity, the so-called readiness potential, began several hundred milliseconds before people reported being aware of their decision. The implication many drew was startling: the brain had, in some sense, already decided before 'you' did. Conscious will looked less like the cause of the action and more like a report arriving after the fact.
Sofia, you're unconvinced.

Profoundly. Libet's experiments are fascinating, but the conclusions drawn from them have been wildly overstated. For one thing, the task is utterly artificial. Flexing your wrist at a random moment for no reason is about as far from a meaningful choice, deciding whether to accept a job, say, or whether to tell the truth, as one could get. More importantly, later work has cast real doubt on what the readiness potential actually represents. A study published about a decade ago suggested it may largely reflect random background fluctuations in neural activity, which happen to cross a threshold, rather than a hidden decision being made. On that reading, there's no secret unconscious choice preceding the conscious one at all.

I accept that the interpretation of the readiness potential is contested. But the broader point doesn't depend on Libet. Everything we know about the brain suggests that it's a physical system obeying physical laws. Our decisions arise from neural processes shaped by our genes, our upbringing and our circumstances, none of which we chose. Where, in that causal chain, is there room for a will that is free in any meaningful sense?

That depends entirely on what you mean by 'free'. If you mean free from all prior causes, then of course we lack it, but I'd argue that notion was always incoherent. A choice that wasn't caused by anything, not even your own values and reasons, would be random, not free. Most philosophers today are what we call compatibilists: they hold that freedom means acting in accordance with your own reasoning and desires, without coercion. And on that definition, neuroscience poses no threat whatsoever. Your reasons are realised in neurons; that doesn't make them any less yours.
Does any of this matter in practical terms?

Enormously, in my view, particularly for the justice system. If we accept that people's behaviour is the product of factors ultimately beyond their control, it becomes much harder to justify punishment as retribution, making people suffer because they 'deserve' it. We'd focus instead on protecting society and on rehabilitation. I'd regard that as a moral advance.

Interestingly, I'd reach a similar policy conclusion by a different route. But I'd caution against telling people they have no free will. There's experimental evidence that participants who read passages arguing that free will is an illusion subsequently behave somewhat less honestly. Whether or not those findings fully replicate, they suggest that our beliefs about agency aren't merely academic. They may shape how we act.

title: The economics of attention to luck

script.t: In today's session I want to explore a question that economists have tended to sidestep, perhaps because the answer is uncomfortable: how much of success is down to luck? Let me begin with a curious statistic. In several countries, if you look at elite professional athletes, a disproportionate number were born in the first few months of the selection year. In Canadian ice hockey, for instance, studies found that players born in January, February and March vastly outnumbered those born in October, November and December. The explanation is mundane. Youth teams group children by calendar year, so a child born in January may be almost twelve months older than a teammate born in December. At the age of eight, that's a substantial physical advantage. The older children are more likely to be selected for the best teams, where they receive better coaching and more practice, so a small initial advantage compounds over time. By adulthood, the difference no longer has anything to do with birth date, but the effect of that early piece of luck persists. Similar patterns have been documented in academic achievement. Now, the point here is not that talent and effort are irrelevant; they clearly matter enormously. It's that small, arbitrary advantages can be amplified by systems that reward early success with further opportunities, what the sociologist Robert Merton called the 'Matthew effect', after the line in the Gospel about those who have being given more. The economist Robert Frank has argued that in what he terms 'winner-take-all' markets, the role of luck is particularly pronounced. In fields like entertainment, technology or publishing, the rewards for being the very best, or the very first, are vastly greater than those for being nearly as good. When many highly talented people compete for a handful of prizes, the winners are almost always both talented and hard-working, but so are many who lose. What separates them is often chance: being in the right place at the right time, a fortunate introduction, a product launched just as the market became ready for it.
But doesn't emphasising luck risk discouraging people from making an effort?

That's the standard objection, and it's an important one. But the evidence suggests something more interesting. Frank cites research indicating that people who are reminded of the role luck played in their success become more generous, more willing to contribute to public goods, without becoming any less motivated. Conversely, those who attribute their success entirely to their own merit tend to be less sympathetic to those who struggle, and less supportive of the public investment, roads, schools, research, from which they themselves benefited. There's also a psychological dimension. Acknowledging luck can be a relief. If success were purely a matter of merit, failure would be purely a matter of personal deficiency, which is a harsh standard to live by. So I'd argue that recognising luck isn't about denying anyone's achievements. It's about seeing the full picture, and that picture has implications for how we think about fairness, taxation and opportunity. For next week, please read Frank's chapter on the subject and come prepared to argue either side.

script.t: Marta Vidal is head of paintings conservation at a major European gallery. Marta, many visitors assume conservation means making old paintings look new again. Is that a misconception?

A very common one. Our first principle is actually to do as little as possible. Every intervention carries a risk, and we're dealing with objects that are irreplaceable. A great deal of my work is preventive: monitoring light levels, humidity and temperature, because fluctuations make canvas and wood expand and contract, which causes paint to crack. When we do intervene, the guiding rule is reversibility. Anything we add, whether varnish or retouching, must be removable by a future conservator without harming the original. We assume, quite rightly, that our successors will know more than we do and may well disagree with our choices.
Can you give an example of that kind of disagreement?

The most famous is probably the cleaning of the Sistine Chapel ceiling in the 1980s and nineties. Michelangelo's frescoes had been covered for centuries by layers of candle smoke, dirt and, crucially, animal glue applied by earlier restorers. When it was removed, the colours that emerged were astonishingly bright: acid greens, vivid pinks and oranges. Some critics were horrified. They argued that the restorers had removed a final layer of shading that Michelangelo himself had applied, and that the dark, sombre Michelangelo that generations had admired had been destroyed. The restorers maintained that the darkness had never been intended. The debate has never been entirely settled, though most specialists now accept that the cleaning was largely justified.
Isn't there a philosophical problem underlying all this? Which version of the painting are you trying to recover?

Exactly, and there's no single right answer. Paintings change over time in ways their creators couldn't control. Certain pigments fade; others darken. Varnishes yellow. Some argue that we should aim for the artist's original intention. But we can rarely know that with certainty, and the passage of time is itself part of the object's history. A painting that has been through four hundred years is a different object from the one that left the studio, and arguably, erasing every trace of age is a kind of falsification. Most conservators today look for a balance: removing later additions that clearly distort the image, while accepting that we can't, and perhaps shouldn't, turn back the clock entirely.
How has technology changed your work?

Profoundly. Infrared imaging lets us see the underdrawing beneath the paint, so we can watch an artist changing their mind, moving a hand, removing a figure. X-rays reveal earlier compositions; we've found entire paintings hidden beneath others, often because canvas was expensive and artists reused it. Chemical analysis of tiny samples tells us exactly which pigments were used, which helps detect forgeries; a supposed seventeenth-century painting containing a pigment that wasn't invented until the nineteenth century is rather difficult to defend. But technology doesn't replace judgement. In the end, every decision involves an aesthetic and ethical choice that no machine can make for us. I tell young conservators that the most important tool in the studio is restraint.

options: It removed shading applied by Michelangelo himself

options: It could be considered a form of falsification
It is always the best option

options: Canvas was expensive, so artists reused it

title: The microbiome
model: Cambridge C2 Proficiency – Listening Part 2 (radio feature)

script.t: Your body is home to trillions of microorganisms, mostly bacteria, living in your gut, on your skin and in your mouth. Collectively known as the microbiome, they were long regarded as passive passengers at best and dangerous invaders at worst. Over the last twenty years, that view has been transformed. Dr Hannah Osei is a microbiologist. Hannah, just how important are these microbes?

Far more important than we imagined. Let me first correct a figure that's often quoted, that bacterial cells outnumber human cells ten to one. More careful recent estimates put the ratio closer to one to one, so it's less dramatic than the headlines suggested, but the numbers are still staggering. And the microbiome contains roughly a hundred times as many genes as the human genome. Those genes allow our microbes to do things our own cells can't, most notably breaking down types of fibre we couldn't otherwise digest, and producing compounds that nourish the cells lining our gut and regulate inflammation. They also train our immune system, particularly in early childhood, teaching it to distinguish between genuine threats and harmless substances.
There's been a great deal of excitement about links between the microbiome and all sorts of conditions.

Yes, and I'd urge a degree of caution. Differences in the microbiome have been associated with obesity, diabetes, allergies, inflammatory bowel disease, and even depression and anxiety. Some of the animal research is genuinely remarkable. Mice raised in completely sterile conditions, with no microbes at all, behave differently and respond to stress differently. And when gut bacteria from obese mice were transferred to lean germ-free mice, the recipients gained more fat than those receiving bacteria from lean donors, despite eating the same diet. But mice are not people, and in humans most of the evidence is correlational. We often don't know whether a particular microbial pattern causes a disease, results from it, or simply reflects some other factor like diet or medication.
Are there treatments that already work?

One stands out. For a severe, recurrent gut infection caused by a bacterium called Clostridioides difficile, which often follows antibiotic treatment, faecal microbiota transplants, essentially transferring gut bacteria from a healthy donor, are strikingly effective, curing around ninety per cent of patients in some studies. That's a far higher success rate than conventional treatment. Beyond that, though, the picture is much less clear. Most commercially available probiotics, for instance, have rather limited evidence behind them for healthy people, and the bacteria they contain often don't establish themselves in the gut for long.
So what can people do to look after their microbiome?

The most consistent finding is that diversity matters, and that the best way to encourage a diverse microbiome is a diverse diet, particularly one rich in different plant foods. One large project found that people who ate more than thirty different types of plants per week had more varied gut bacteria than those who ate ten or fewer. Fermented foods such as yoghurt, kefir and kimchi also seem to help. And, of course, avoid unnecessary antibiotics, which can disrupt the microbial community for months.

options: Bacteria are fewer than human cells
It is closer to one to one than often claimed

questions.prompt: Which function of the microbiome does she mention?

options: They gained more fat on the same diet

options: It has already solved most diseases

script.t: Every generation seems to believe the language is going to the dogs. With me are linguist Professor Eleanor Hughes and Graham Fowler, editor of a well-known style guide. Graham, are you worried about the state of English?

Worried is perhaps too strong. But I do think standards matter. When people write 'could of' instead of 'could have', or use 'literally' to mean 'figuratively', clarity suffers. A shared standard allows us to communicate across regions, classes and generations. If everyone simply does what they like, that common ground erodes.

I'd question some of that. Take 'literally'. People have been using it as an intensifier for more than two hundred years. You'll find it in Dickens, in Mark Twain. It's not a recent corruption. And context almost always makes the meaning clear; nobody who hears 'I literally died laughing' calls an ambulance. Words that mean 'truly' tend to weaken over time into general intensifiers. The same thing happened to 'very', which originally meant 'truly', from the same root as 'verify', and to 'really'. That's not decay. It's one of the most regular patterns in the history of language.
But surely there's a difference between natural evolution and simple error? 'Could of' arises because people mishear 'could've'. It isn't a new meaning; it's a mistake.

In writing, I'd agree it's non-standard, and I'd correct it in a student essay. But notice that it tells us something interesting: that for many speakers, 'could've' has become a single unit, and the 'have' is no longer felt as a separate word. Linguists are interested in why these things happen rather than in condemning them. And historically, many forms we now consider perfectly correct began life as errors. 'An apron' was originally 'a napron'; people misdivided the words. Nobody today would call 'apron' a mistake.
Graham, does that convince you?

Partly. I accept that meanings shift. But I'd point out that a reader in a formal context may still judge the writer harshly for using it, fairly or not. Part of a style guide's job is to protect writers from that kind of judgement, whatever linguists think about it.
So is there any role for style guides, in your view?

Absolutely, as long as they're honest about what they are. Advice about what's appropriate in formal writing is valuable; students and professionals need to know the conventions. What I object to is presenting arbitrary preferences as rules of logic. The prohibition on splitting infinitives, 'to boldly go', was invented by eighteenth-century grammarians who thought English should behave like Latin, where infinitives are single words and can't be split. There was never any good reason for it.

I'll concede the split infinitive. Our guide abandoned that rule years ago. But I'd still argue that someone needs to defend distinctions that carry meaning. 'Disinterested' meaning impartial and 'uninterested' meaning bored is a useful distinction, and it's being lost.

That's a fair example, and I share your affection for it. Though, ironically, 'disinterested' was used to mean 'not interested' in the seventeenth century, before the distinction you're defending became established. Languages lose some distinctions and create others. Ultimately, usage is decided not by editors or professors but by millions of speakers.
Which is precisely why someone has to speak up for clarity.

options: English is borrowing too many words
Losing a shared standard harms clear communication

questions.prompt: What point does Eleanor make about 'literally'?
options: It has been used as an intensifier for centuries

options: Some correct forms originated as mistakes

title: The carbon footprint of the internet

script.t: We tend to think of the digital world as somehow weightless, existing in 'the cloud'. Dr Lukas Brandt studies the environmental impact of information technology. Lukas, is the cloud really as clean as it sounds?

The metaphor is wonderfully misleading. The cloud is in fact a vast physical infrastructure: millions of servers in data centres, thousands of kilometres of undersea cables, mobile phone networks, and of course the billions of devices we hold in our hands. All of it consumes electricity, and manufacturing the devices consumes raw materials and energy. Estimates vary considerably, but the information and communications sector is generally thought to account for somewhere between two and four per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions, roughly comparable to the aviation industry.
There have been some dramatic headlines, for instance, that streaming a video for half an hour produces as much carbon as driving several kilometres.

Yes, and that particular figure turned out to be wildly exaggerated. Later analysis suggested it was overstated by a factor of something like fifty, partly because it used outdated assumptions about how much energy data transmission requires. Networks have become enormously more efficient. That's an important point, because sensational numbers can backfire. People start feeling guilty about sending an email, which is almost irrelevant, while ignoring decisions that genuinely matter.
So what does genuinely matter?

For individuals, the single biggest factor by far is the manufacture of devices. For a typical smartphone, the great majority of its lifetime carbon footprint comes from production, mining the metals, making the chips, assembling and shipping it, rather than from charging it or using data. So the most effective thing a consumer can do is to keep devices for longer. Extending the life of a phone from two years to four makes a much bigger difference than any change in how you use it. That's why the campaigns for a 'right to repair', requiring manufacturers to make spare parts and repair information available, are so significant.
What about the data centres themselves?

They've become remarkably efficient, partly because energy is a major cost for the companies that run them. Many large operators now buy renewable electricity and locate data centres in cold climates, to reduce the energy needed for cooling. Some even use waste heat to warm nearby homes. The concern now is the very rapid growth in demand, driven particularly by artificial intelligence. Training and running large AI models requires enormous computing power, and in some regions, the expansion of data centres is putting real pressure on electricity grids and water supplies, since many use water for cooling. Efficiency gains have so far largely kept pace with growth in demand, but there's no guarantee that will continue.
Is there a risk of what economists call a rebound effect?

Very much so. When something becomes cheaper and more efficient, we tend to use more of it, sometimes so much more that total consumption rises. It's an old observation, dating back to the nineteenth century and coal. Digital efficiency gains are undoubtedly real, but whether they reduce overall emissions depends on choices we make collectively, about energy sources, about regulation and about what we actually need.

options: It is actually a huge physical infrastructure

script.t: Few institutions have captured the imagination like the Great Library of Alexandria. Founded in the third century BC by the Ptolemies, the Greek dynasty that ruled Egypt after Alexander the Great, it aimed to collect every book in the known world. Its destruction, in a single catastrophic fire, has become a symbol of lost knowledge and of the fragility of civilisation. Yet according to historians, much of that story is myth. Dr Yasmin Farouk is a historian of the ancient world.

The library was certainly real, and certainly extraordinary. The Ptolemies pursued books with remarkable determination. There's a well-known anecdote that every ship arriving in Alexandria was searched for books, which were then copied; the library kept the originals and returned the copies to the owners. Another story claims the Ptolemies borrowed the official Athenian texts of the great tragedies, paying an enormous deposit, and then simply kept them, sacrificing the money. Whether every detail is true, we can't say, but they convey the ambition. Estimates of the collection range from forty thousand to several hundred thousand scrolls, though ancient figures are notoriously unreliable. And it wasn't just a store of books. Scholars working there measured the circumference of the Earth with impressive accuracy, edited the definitive texts of Homer and produced the first major translation of the Hebrew scriptures into Greek.
So what happened to it?

This is where popular history goes astray. The dramatic version usually blames one of three culprits: Julius Caesar, whose troops set fire to ships in the harbour in 48 BC; Christian mobs in the fourth century AD; or the Arab conquest in the seventh century. The last of these accounts, in which a caliph supposedly ordered the books to be burned, appears only centuries after the event and is rejected by most historians as a later invention. Caesar's fire probably did destroy some books, perhaps warehouses near the docks, but the library evidently continued to function afterwards, because scholars are recorded working there long after. What most historians now believe is far less cinematic: a slow decline over several centuries. Royal funding dried up as the Ptolemaic dynasty weakened and Egypt became a Roman province. In 145 BC, a ruler expelled many intellectuals from the city. Papyrus scrolls decay, particularly in a humid climate, and need to be recopied every few decades; when the money and the scholars disappeared, so did the copying.
Why, then, has the myth of the great fire proved so durable?

Partly because a single dramatic catastrophe makes a better story than gradual neglect. Partly because each version of the myth has served someone's purposes: Enlightenment writers, for instance, used it to portray religion as the enemy of reason. But I think there's a more uncomfortable reason. The idea of a sudden fire lets us off the hook. The real lesson of Alexandria is that knowledge is rarely lost in a single blaze. It's lost when societies stop paying for libraries, stop valuing scholarship and stop maintaining what they've inherited. That should give us pause in an era when so much of our knowledge is stored in digital formats that become unreadable within decades unless they're actively preserved.

script.t: Should every adult receive a regular, unconditional payment from the state, whether or not they work? With me are Rebecca Stone, an economist who supports a universal basic income, and David Marsh, a former government adviser who has doubts. Rebecca, make your case.

The central argument is that our welfare systems were designed for a world of stable, lifelong employment, which no longer exists for millions of people. Today's benefits are complex, means-tested and often stigmatising. People who take on a few hours of extra work can lose more in benefits than they gain in wages, which is a powerful disincentive. A basic income removes that trap, because you keep it regardless of what you earn. It also recognises the enormous amount of unpaid work, caring for children and elderly relatives, volunteering, that our economy depends on but doesn't reward. And with automation likely to disrupt many occupations, it offers a floor beneath which nobody can fall.
David?

I share the diagnosis that the current system has serious flaws. My doubts concern the cure. The first is cost. If you give every adult an amount that's actually enough to live on, the price is enormous, typically estimated at a substantial share of national income. Paying for it would require large tax rises. If, on the other hand, you make the payment affordable, it's too small to replace existing benefits, so you end up keeping the complex system alongside it. The second concern is targeting. A universal payment goes to millionaires as well as to people in poverty. Spending the same money on those who need it most would arguably do far more to reduce hardship.

On targeting, the money paid to wealthy people would largely be recovered through the tax system, so in practice it's not as wasteful as it sounds. And universality has a value of its own: it removes stigma and the bureaucracy needed to check eligibility.
That's true in theory, but it makes the headline cost and the required tax rises even more politically difficult.
What about the worry that people would stop working?

The evidence from trials, in Finland, in Kenya, in various cities in the United States, is fairly consistent: employment falls very little, if at all. In some cases it rises. What does change is wellbeing. In the Finnish trial, recipients reported less stress and greater trust in institutions. Some people use the security to retrain, start businesses or leave abusive situations.

I'd be careful about drawing too much from those trials. They were temporary and limited, and people behave differently when they know a payment will end in two years than they would if it were permanent. Nor do small pilots tell us what happens to prices, wages and tax revenue when an entire country adopts the policy. I'm not opposed to further experiments. But I'd sooner see targeted reforms, simplifying benefits and ending the penalties for taking on work, which would capture many of the advantages Rebecca describes at a fraction of the cost.
Those reforms would certainly help. I just doubt they'd go far enough.

script.t: We tend to imagine memory as a kind of video recording, stored somewhere in the brain and replayed when we need it. Decades of research have shown that this picture is fundamentally mistaken. Remembering is not retrieval; it is reconstruction. Each time we recall an event, we rebuild it from fragments, filling the gaps with expectations, general knowledge and information acquired later. And in doing so, we can alter the memory itself. Some of the most influential work in this area was carried out by the psychologist Elizabeth Loftus. In a classic experiment in the 1970s, participants watched film of a car accident and were then asked how fast the cars were going when they 'hit' each other, or, for other groups, when they 'smashed into', 'collided with' or 'contacted' each other. The wording dramatically affected their estimates; 'smashed' produced the highest speeds. A week later, participants who had heard 'smashed' were more than twice as likely to report having seen broken glass, although there had been none. A single word had changed what they remembered seeing. Loftus went further. In what became known as the 'lost in the mall' study, she and her colleagues showed that it was possible to implant memories of entire events that had never happened. Participants were given short descriptions of childhood events supposedly provided by family members. Most were true, but one, getting lost in a shopping centre as a young child, was invented. After repeated interviews, around a quarter of participants came to remember the false event, sometimes in vivid detail. Crucially, false memories can feel exactly as real and as certain as true ones. Confidence is not a reliable indicator of accuracy, a finding with profound implications for the legal system. In the United States, analyses of convictions later overturned by DNA evidence have found that mistaken eyewitness identification played a role in the majority of cases. Witnesses were not lying. They genuinely believed what they remembered.
So should courts simply stop relying on eyewitness evidence?

Not entirely; eyewitnesses are often right, and in some cases they're the only evidence. But the research has led to important reforms in many places. Police line-ups should be conducted by an officer who doesn't know which person is the suspect, so they can't unconsciously give cues. Witnesses should be told that the culprit may not be present. And their confidence should be recorded immediately, at the first identification, because confidence tends to grow over time, especially if they receive feedback such as 'Good, you picked our suspect.' An initial hesitant identification that becomes certain in the courtroom months later should be treated with great caution. More broadly, I think this research should make all of us a little humbler. The vivid memory of an argument with a partner, or of where you were when you heard some important news, may be far less accurate than it feels. Studies of so-called flashbulb memories, of events like major disasters, show that people's accounts change substantially over the years, while their confidence remains as high as ever.

script.t: Quantum computing is constantly in the headlines, often described as a technology that will revolutionise everything from medicine to finance. Dr Mei Tanaka is a quantum physicist. Mei, can you explain, in plain language, what makes a quantum computer different?

I'll try, though I should warn you that plain language and quantum mechanics don't always get along. An ordinary computer stores information in bits, each of which is either a zero or a one. A quantum computer uses quantum bits, or qubits, which can exist in what's called a superposition, a combination of zero and one at the same time, until they're measured. Qubits can also be entangled, meaning their states are linked so that what happens to one is connected to the other, however far apart they are. The popular explanation is that a quantum computer therefore tries every possible answer at once. That's not really accurate, and it creates unrealistic expectations. What actually happens is subtler: a well-designed quantum algorithm makes the different possibilities interfere with each other, rather like waves, so that wrong answers cancel out and the right answer is reinforced. That only works for certain kinds of problems.
Which kinds?

The most promising application, in my view, is simulating nature itself, molecules and materials, which are governed by quantum mechanics. Ordinary computers struggle enormously with this, because the complexity grows exponentially with the number of particles. A quantum computer could help design new medicines, better batteries or more efficient methods of producing fertiliser, which currently consumes a significant fraction of the world's energy. There's also a famous algorithm that could, in principle, break much of the encryption that currently protects internet communications and banking. That's why governments and companies are already introducing new 'post-quantum' encryption methods, designed to resist such attacks, even though no machine capable of it exists yet. Information that's intercepted today could be stored and decrypted in the future.
Why don't we have powerful quantum computers already?

Because qubits are incredibly fragile. The slightest disturbance, a tiny vibration, a change in temperature, stray electromagnetic radiation, can destroy their quantum state, a process called decoherence. Many current machines have to be cooled to a fraction of a degree above absolute zero, colder than outer space. And errors accumulate rapidly. To perform long, reliable calculations, we'll need error correction, which means combining many physical qubits, perhaps a thousand or more, to create a single reliable 'logical' qubit. We've made genuine progress on that in the last few years, but we're still some distance from the millions of high-quality qubits that the most ambitious applications would require.
So is the hype justified?

Partly. The science is real, and I'm genuinely excited about it. But there's been a tendency, encouraged by investment pressures, to announce breakthroughs that turn out to be narrower than claimed, for instance, a quantum computer solving a problem faster than a supercomputer, when the problem has been specifically chosen and has no practical use. Quantum computers won't replace your laptop; for most everyday tasks they'd be worse. My honest prediction is that they'll become specialised tools, transformative in certain fields, irrelevant in most others, and that the timescale will be longer than the enthusiasts suggest, but shorter than the sceptics claim.
